title: Russian Hackers Stole Emails and 2FA Codes Via Zimbra Flaw With No User Clicks Required
excerpt: A multi-nation advisory blamed Russian group Laundry Bear for a cyberespionage campaign that compromised Zimbra email accounts the moment users opened a malicious message.
body:
• The U.S. and over a dozen allied nations attributed a cyberespionage campaign to Russian government-backed group Laundry Bear, which stole emails by exploiting a Zimbra vulnerability that required no user interaction beyond opening an email.
  • The "half-click exploit" harvested credentials, session tokens, backup 2FA codes, browser-saved passwords, and 90 days of mailbox contents — all exfiltrated over DNS and HTTPS channels.
  • The campaign first targeted Ukrainian government agencies, including critical infrastructure, before expanding to hit users across NATO member states.
  • A U.S. indictment tied the hacking group to Russian cybersecurity firm Yutek-NN, whose deputy director was arrested in Thailand and faces charges in Boston.

The United States and more than a dozen allied nations on Thursday blamed a Russian government-supported hacking group for a cyberespionage campaign that stole emails from users of the Zimbra email platform — without requiring victims to click a link or open an attachment.

The technique, which cybersecurity firm Proofpoint described as a "half-click exploit," leveraged a now-patched vulnerability in Zimbra Collaboration Suite (tracked as CVE-2025-66376) that allowed attackers to compromise accounts the moment a user simply opened a malicious email in a vulnerable webmail session, according to Reuters.

How the Attack Worked

The vulnerability, a stored cross-site scripting (XSS) flaw, enabled attackers to embed an obfuscated JavaScript payload directly in the HTML body of an email. No malicious attachments, no suspicious links, no macros — the entire attack chain lived inside a single email message, according to research by Seqrite Labs, which first documented the campaign as "Operation GhostMail."

https://x.com/DailyDarkWeb/status/2080582208952193416

"The script executes silently in the browser and begins harvesting credentials, session tokens, backup 2FA codes, browser-saved passwords, and the contents of the victim's mailbox going back 90 days."

— Seqrite Labs researchers

The stolen data was exfiltrated through both DNS and HTTPS channels, making detection more difficult. The malware also manipulated Zimbra's email filter rules to redirect all inbound and outbound messages to an attacker-controlled Proton Mail address, establishing persistent access even after the initial breach.

Who Was Targeted

A 31-page joint advisory from police and intelligence agencies in the U.S., Netherlands, Canada, Britain, Australia, New Zealand, Denmark, the Czech Republic, and other European nations attributed the campaign to Laundry Bear, one of several hacking groups the U.S. alleges work for Russian security services.

The campaign heavily targeted Ukraine first, including the State Hydrographic Service — a critical infrastructure entity under Ukraine's Ministry of Infrastructure. It then expanded to hit users in the United States and other NATO member nations.

"It's particularly concerning that these thugs tested their methods on victims in Ukraine, before targeting members of NATO," British Security Minister Dan Jarvis said in a statement.

The Yutek-NN Connection

A U.S. indictment filed this month tied Laundry Bear to a Russian cybersecurity company called Yutek-NN. The firm's deputy director, Denis Obrezko, faces hacking-related charges in Boston following his arrest in Thailand last year. He has pleaded not guilty. The Russian embassy in Washington did not respond to requests for comment, and Yutek-NN has not addressed the allegations. Moscow typically denies involvement in hacking campaigns.

A Pattern of Zimbra Exploitation

Zimbra, a widely used email and collaboration platform with hundreds of millions of users including government agencies and businesses worldwide, has become a recurring target for Russian state-sponsored hackers. In 2023, the Winter Vivern cyberespionage group used a different XSS exploit to breach Zimbra portals and spy on NATO-aligned officials, military personnel, and diplomats, according to BleepingComputer. In October 2024, U.S. and U.K. agencies warned that APT29 hackers linked to Russia's Foreign Intelligence Service were attacking vulnerable Zimbra servers "at a mass scale."

What It Means for Organizations

For Indian government agencies and enterprises that rely on Zimbra for email — a common choice due to its open-source licensing and cost advantages — the advisory is a direct call to action. The vulnerability has been patched in Zimbra versions 10.0.18 and 10.1.13, and CISA has ordered U.S. federal agencies to secure their servers within two weeks. Organizations still running unpatched Zimbra instances should update immediately and review mail filters for unauthorized changes.
